assumptions: The initial beachhead is Polish small and mid-sized DORA-scope financial entities whose register workflow is not already controlled by a group GRC platform or an incumbent product.
The offer is a standardized annual software and data-quality service priced within the stated 12,000-36,000 PLN range, with bounded onboarding and exception review rather than open-ended consulting.

Security-approved access to confidential contracts, appropriate EU data handling, specialist DORA review, and liability protection are obtainable but unproven; their absence is treated as uncertainty rather than as evidence of impossibility.
The founder keeps the corporate job during validation, contributes at most 3-5 hours per day, and uses contractors or advisors for legal, security, and compliance expertise that AI cannot replace.
No audit or compliance partner commitment, buyer budget, extraction-accuracy result, procurement duration, retention result, or customer traction is assumed beyond the supplied evidence.
The illustrative 300-customer wealth path is a scenario, not evidence that the reachable market or acquisition engine can support that scale.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A binding, interlinked reporting obligation applied to fragmented ICT contracts creates a real reconciliation and error-repair gate, and the official dry run plus Polish resubmissions show that the problem is not merely hypothetical. The insight is useful but fairly visible, already productized by several vendors, and not yet sharpened into a uniquely controlled workflow.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Regulated entities must produce the register, and the 6.5% all-check pass rate and rejected Polish submissions establish meaningful accuracy pain. Transparent competitor prices make recurring payment plausible, but they do not prove demand for this entrant; free official spreadsheets, capable internal GRC teams, and learning after early filing cycles may reduce both urgency and recurring willingness to pay.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Annual pricing of 12,000-36,000 PLN and software-like delivery could support attractive gross margin, and recurring contract changes provide a basis for retention. However, CAC, sales-cycle length, payback, renewal, partner share, human exception cost, security cost, insurance, and real extraction accuracy are all unknown. The 300-entity founder-wealth path is arithmetically plausible but commercially demanding, while expert review or bespoke remediation could erode both margin and operating leverage.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Smaller Polish DORA entities with fragmented contract records and outsourced compliance form a coherent first segment, especially if one partner can aggregate several accounts. The supplied evidence does not quantify reachable unserved entities, approved budgets, contract counts, or how many are already covered by group tools, internal workflows, or incumbents; therefore the beachhead's ability to support hundreds of customers remains uncertain.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: DAPR is an exact Warsaw-based substitute with automated validation and supply-chain handling, while Vendorica already offers AI extraction and a live vendor-contract-asset graph and ReportAct supplies a lower-entry alternative. Official forms are a further substitute. Without exclusive channel access, materially superior accuracy, or a narrower proprietary control point, a new entrant has little demonstrated basis for dominating even the proposed local niche.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A trusted contract and provider data layer could extend into continuous vendor-risk monitoring, change workflows, incident support, broader DORA modules, adjacent regulations, and additional EU geographies. Those adjacencies are logically related and could reuse data, but they also move directly into broader GRC territory where established vendors already have product breadth and customer trust.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Verified provider identities, field mappings, correction history, integrations, and workflow embedding could create modest learning effects and switching cost. Yet confidential customer contracts limit reusable cross-customer data, template rules are public, the proposed graph overlaps incumbent capabilities, and extraction or validation features are readily copied unless the entrant secures privileged portfolio distribution or a demonstrably superior proprietary correction corpus.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Evidence-linked extraction, rapid rejected-cell repair, and partner delivery could improve review speed and trust, but these are hypotheses rather than measured advantages. No field-level accuracy, review-time reduction, lower total cost, faster onboarding, or reliability result shows a behavior-changing advantage, and the closest incumbents already claim substantially overlapping automation.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: DORA's recent implementation, poor dry-run quality, and 2025 resubmissions create a timely window while entities are still operationalizing the obligation. The window is not unambiguously expanding: organizations may learn the process after initial cycles, official guidance is improving, and several purpose-built vendors are already in market.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A free preflight tool and a Polish audit or compliance partner could produce portfolio-level acquisition, reduce CAC, and fit the founder's preference for low-social-energy selling. No partner commitment or channel economics exists, partners may prefer spreadsheets or incumbents, and each regulated buyer may still impose a long security and procurement review. Repeatable, affordable acquisition is therefore plausible but currently structurally unsecured.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Entity resolution, extraction, validation, and analytics fit the founder well, and a synthetic-data validator is feasible part-time with AI leverage and the stated capital. Production delivery is materially harder: multilingual contract accuracy, legal interpretation, confidential-data security, insurance, regulator-facing reliability, specialist oversight, procurement, and error liability cannot be automated away and may exceed a five-hour daily schedule or 80,000 PLN before repeatable revenue.

main_structural_strength: The product sits at a mandatory, objectively testable reporting-quality gate where official failure and resubmission evidence demonstrates real operational pain, and the founder's data-extraction and validation skills match a narrow prototype unusually well.
primary_score_limiter: There is no demonstrated material advantage or controlled distribution channel against an exact local incumbent, two additional priced substitutes, and a free internal workflow; this makes the otherwise plausible SaaS economics and founder-wealth path depend on simultaneous unproven channel, accuracy, and retention assumptions.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: DAPR already sells an exact Warsaw-based DORA register product with automation, validation, provider dependencies, and supply-chain data, while Vendorica already combines AI agreement extraction with the proposed live vendor-contract graph. This directly contradicts the thesis that those features alone create a differentiated entry wedge.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Obtain a paid pilot or binding portfolio commitment from a compliance or audit partner; benchmark field-level precision, exception-review minutes, and regulator-format pass rates on representative multilingual contracts against both manual work and at least one incumbent; document security and procurement requirements; and measure buyer price acceptance, partner share, onboarding effort, contract-change frequency, renewal intent, CAC, and expected payback across several independent entities.
highest_value_structural_change: Recast the company as a white-label, partner-embedded rejected-register repair and evidence-linked QA layer, and build only after one audit or compliance partner commits a paid multi-entity portfolio with minimum annual volume. This would turn the critical distribution dependency into contracted aggregation, narrow the product away from full-suite incumbent competition, and concentrate proprietary learning on verified exceptions and rejection patterns.
